doc.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview

chapter: Riverside and the New York scene
title: Stan Getz fires Ware for playing too much bass
summary: At Birdland with Getz and Elvin Jones, Ware is let go after one set; Keepnews phones Getz and the union makes him pay.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: And he called me up for a gig -- Mr. Stan Getz, and Elvin Jones, Wynton Elmer, Joe Kelly and myself, and we were working -- that's Red Garland, Philly Joe, Trane, Paul, and himself opposite the Miles Davis Quintet -- at Birdland.

Naturally, we were gonna cook -- we were gonna play our best, too, and not realizing, you know, Stan Getz -- he's a star; naturally he's a star, but we want to get behind and push him just as much; the rhythm section was pushing Miles. And I don't know, Stan was going through his little problems during that time, and the other one was playing all those poly-rhythms, and Stan was getting confused; he didn't know what to do, so after the first set, we come off the bandstand, and he says, "Elvin" and Elton turned around and said, "What?" And Stan said, "Nothing" and then looked over at me and say, "Oh, Wilbur? I want to try another bass player." And I said, "Well what for?" and he said, "Well, I do, man?" I just want to try another bass" and I said all right.
So the next time, I was in line for the Riverside Keepnews for my daily sleevng job, and he says what happened, and I said, "Well, Stan said he was gonna try another bass player.'

He said, 'What have you done?' He was thinking that I was goofing off or messing up, so I said, 'Call him up and ask him'. So, he picks up the phone, and he gives me the phone; I said I want to learn myself; I figured Stan would tell him what the trouble was.

So he picks up the phone and says to Stan, 'What happened? Why you let Wilbur go?' and he said, 'Oh, he's playing too much.' And he says, 'Playing too much?' -- and he says, 'Yeah, he's playing too much bass.' -- so he says, 'Okay'. So somebody say, well, he can't do that. Go tell the union. Now he say he was trying out another bass player each night, he was trying out different bass players, and it wasn't the bass player's fault; it was just that they were playing all that one and three different rhythms and he didn't know where it was at, and as I say, Stan was going through problems, personal problems, and ...
But that shouldn't ... should that affect the music?

It didn't affect the music, I mean, you know the personality of the individual musician, but it didn't look right to people, you know. But anyway, Louie made him pay me for the two weeks, enough for the week, and I only played one set. But see, then, Chicago Sound, and working around different people. Oh, I worked with Buddy Rich during that time, too, and Gene Quill and Phil Woods
There was a certain amount of temperament going on. the union
